transcript: This is the Innovative Workforce, where we explore, question, and share ideas about the reinvention of the modern workforce. My name is Craig von Kullenberg, and I am the Executive Director of the Governor's Office of Workforce Innovation for the State of Nevada. Workforce development. Have you ever heard the same word or phrase repeated so many times that it just starts to lose its meaning? Over the last seven years, I have sat through a lot of meetings. Sometimes I led the meetings, sometimes I just participated, other times I just listened. But the central theme to all these meetings has been workforce development. I have to tell you, sometimes the phrase just makes me cringe, which is funny because the bio that I submit for events says that I am a passionate workforce development professional, which is actually true. Let me explain. There are advanced theories, books, websites, classes, even doctorate degrees that focus primarily on workforce development. All these resources are meant to train people to accomplish two goals. One, provide career pathways to people, and two, to provide skilled, qualified workforce for industry. In the end, businesses should increase their retention and profitability, and individuals should grow in their careers in prosperity. These are the things that I am passionate about. I truly believe that workforce development, when it's done right, is the shortest path from poverty to prosperity. But here's the reason that the phrase makes me want to bang my head against the wall sometimes. Our country and our state have invested literally billions of dollars, and incalculable time into the workforce development system. We have state workforce development boards, state agencies, local workforce development boards, community colleges, private colleges, training providers, mandated workforce development partners, all working towards these goals. We gather data to track our efforts. We report it out, and we pat ourselves on the back for the difference we're making in people's lives. But when all the praise and adulation is done, and I drive home, I'm still driving through neighborhoods with extremely high unemployment rates. I know that our efforts have put some people in jobs where they actually lose money because their wages don't cover the benefits that they're losing. I know that our efforts have barely moved the needle on income equality, inequality, and workplace diversity. I know that while our programming may have given a person an entry-level job, they haven't gotten the social, emotional resiliency they need to utilize their entry-level position to launch a lifelong career. I know that in many ways we have failed the people that we serve. And in the end, I'm just tired of having the same conversations over and over again about workforce development. Now, I want everyone to understand, I'm not criticizing the people that work in this world. Everyone that I work with here in the office of Owen, and with all of our other workforce development partners, I know that they're all passionate about the work and probably experience the same frustration that I do. But there are some inherent flaws in our society that contribute to the problem. The main problem as I see it is that we face is the backward approach that we tend to take toward the workforce development. It's an educational system that works best when run by employers. Now, historically speaking, workforce development was the job of the companies that employ people. It wasn't up to government entities, community colleges, or other providers to create a workforce for companies. At some point, and probably with great intentions, the government and educational system decided to get in the game. I can tell you with 100% certainty that when the government and/or the colleges decide that they know what the employer needs better than the employer does, there's going to be a problem. There has to be a shift in the system where employers are not just directly involved in the design of the programming, but are actually leading it. Another problem that we face is the separation between education and workforce development. I can't explain the reasoning behind it, but there's a wall that has been put between the two. When a child is taught to add and subtract, aren't they gaining a workforce skill? When a doctor is learning to perform neurosurgery at college, are they not being prepared for the workforce? When I was taught to use a mathematics formula to calculate the offset needed to make two sections of ductwork connect, wasn't I being educated? Now, there's this thing that I like to call educational hubris that exists in our society where academic pursuits, including the gaining of a college degree, are considered superior to training in hands-on blue collar trades. This causes workforce development efforts to be looked at with disdain and forced on those that are deemed not good enough for college. But if we could find a way to once again merge education and workforce development and then contextualize the educational system to marketable workforce skills, I think we could create graduates at all levels that are actually ready to go to work. Last problem that I want to talk about today is the general lack of employability skills and resiliency in today's workforce. When we engage with employers and ask about the skills that are lacking in their workers, the answers almost always include basic skills that a lot of people believe should be inherent in a modern society. Punctuality, focus, communication, teamwork, these are a few of the skills that are apparently lacking. You know, maybe it's a question for psychologists to figure out, but the foundation of these skills lies in social emotional learning that is generally lacking in both our educational and our workforce development system. We haven't adequately figured out how to teach the importance of being to work on time and staying off your phone while you're there. In fact, many would argue that these skills can't be taught in a classroom, but should be taught at home. I don't necessarily believe that, but I'm not going to go down the psychology and sociology rabbit hole now, but it is an interesting discussion. Now of course, these are just a few of the issues that hurt the workforce development system and ultimately keep me from sleeping at night. We haven't even gotten into the bureaucracy of the Weo system. I know that the answers to these and other questions about the system exist. We just need to find them. Maybe I'm tired of hearing a phrase so many times that its meeting gets lost in the whirlwind of our daily activities. I mean, I've certainly said it enough times in this podcast, but I do remain passionate about helping those that I serve and finding new ways to serve more people. Thank you for listening today. Thanks for listening to
